title: File-Based Routing
summary: Folders and special files in the app directory can create Next.js routes.

subtopics.title: Route segments
subtopics.explanation: A folder adds a route segment, and a `page.tsx` file makes that route render a page. For example, `products/page.tsx` maps to `/products`. It is like an address made from street names. A folder alone does not always create a page, so check the special files that define the route. Folders describe URL structure, while special files describe what renders. Keep both responsibilities visible so a route can be found by looking at the source tree.

subtopics.title: Page file
subtopics.explanation: A `page.tsx` file contains the route’s page component. Keep route-specific content and behavior here. Visiting the URL directly or refreshing it should still render the page. For example, a product route should work when someone pastes `/products` into a new tab, not only after clicking a link in the app. Page components can load or receive data for their route, but should handle missing records explicitly. A valid URL pattern does not mean the requested resource exists. A page file is like the room placed at the address named by its folders.

subtopics.title: Shared layout
subtopics.explanation: A `layout.tsx` file wraps pages beneath its route segment. It can hold shared navigation or a sidebar. It is like a hallway connecting several rooms. Place a component in a layout when it is truly shared; keep page-only forms and messages in the page so unrelated routes do not inherit them. Layouts persist around child pages, so place shared shell elements there and avoid coupling unrelated pages to state they do not need.

subtopics.title: Dynamic route
subtopics.explanation: A dynamic folder such as `[slug]` matches different values in one part of a route. An article page can use the slug to find the requested article. Treat that value as input: check that it is valid and that the record exists before rendering. A dynamic path does not automatically validate data or permissions. Route parameters are external input. Validate format, handle not-found cases, and perform authorization before exposing a record. A dynamic segment is like a street address template with one changing house number.

subtopics.title: Private organization
subtopics.explanation: A route group can organize related files without adding the group name to the public URL. A folder without a page can also organize code. These conventions are like labels on a filing cabinet. Verify the final address from the route files, then test direct visits, refresh, Back, and Forward. Use direct navigation tests to catch paths that work only after client-side transitions. Check refresh, browser history, and unknown segments.

foundations.overview: The Next.js App Router builds URLs from folders and special files. A folder adds a route segment, while `page.tsx` makes the route display a page. Think of folders as street names and page files as doors at those addresses. Dynamic folders match changing values, and organization-only folders can keep code tidy without changing the URL.
foundations.whyItMatters: The file tree is part of the routing model. Understanding which files create routes and which only organize code prevents confusing URL behavior.
foundations.browserPerspective: When a user navigates, Next.js resolves the URL to the matching folder, composes the layouts from the root down, and renders the leaf page. Shared layouts persist across navigations, so the browser only swaps the changing segment rather than reloading the whole shell.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Marketing sites use route groups to organize sections, blogs use dynamic [slug] segments, dashboards use nested layouts for persistent sidebars, and every app uses page.tsx files to expose its routes — all driven by folder structure.
foundations.businessImpact: Predictable, convention-based routing speeds up development and onboarding because the URL map is self-documenting, reducing time spent wiring and debugging routing configuration.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Engineers reason about routes by browsing folders, colocate route-specific code naturally, and get loading/error states by convention — but they must learn which filenames are reserved and how segments compose.
foundations.performanceImpact: Per-segment code splitting means each route loads only its own JS, and loading.tsx enables streaming so users see content sooner. Layouts persist across navigation, avoiding redundant re-rendering of shared shells.
commonUseCases: Exposing pages by adding page.tsx to a folder (e.g. app/pricing/page.tsx -> /pricing)
Nested layouts for persistent navigation in dashboards
Route groups (parentheses) to organize sections without changing URLs
Colocating route-specific components and helpers inside the route folder

commonMisconceptions.myth: Every file in a route folder becomes a route.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Only reserved files (page, layout, loading, error, not-found, route) are routing files; other files are safely colocated and ignored by the router.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A folder by itself creates a visitable URL.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A folder is just a segment; it only becomes a navigable route when it contains a page.tsx.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Every folder creates a public route.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A page file is required for a route; some folders only organize source files.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A dynamic segment is already a validated database identifier.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Route parameters are input and should be checked before use in queries or authorization.

visualExplorer.title: How a folder tree becomes URLs
visualExplorer.caption: Step from the app/ directory down to a rendered route.

config.intro: Walk the file system and watch each piece map to the URL and UI.

steps.name: app/ root
steps.detail: Everything routable lives under app/. The root layout.tsx wraps the whole app and defines <html>/<body>.

steps.name: Folder = segment
steps.detail: Each folder under app/ is a route segment; its name becomes a part of the URL path.

steps.name: page.tsx = route
steps.detail: Adding a page.tsx to a segment makes it a navigable URL; its default export is the page UI.

steps.name: Nesting
steps.detail: Nested folders create nested URLs, and each level can add its own layout/loading/error files.

steps.name: Special files
steps.detail: layout wraps children, loading shows a Suspense fallback, error catches failures, not-found handles misses.

steps.name: Colocation
steps.detail: Non-reserved files (components, helpers, tests) sit beside the route and are ignored by the router.

interactiveExamples.title: Map a folder tree to URLs (runnable)
interactiveExamples.explanation: This runnable demo computes the URL each page.tsx produces from a folder tree — the same logic Next.js uses. Route groups in parentheses are stripped from the URL.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Each file path mapped to its URL: /, /about, /pricing (group stripped), /blog/:slug.

interactiveExamples.title: Special files of a segment (illustrative)
interactiveExamples.explanation: This illustrative demo lists the reserved special files Next.js recognizes in a route segment and what each does. In a real project these are actual files on disk.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A list of the reserved special files (layout, page, loading, error, not-found) and their roles.

codeLab.title: Predict the URL for each file
codeLab.instructions: For each file path, fill in the URL it produces in the App Router. Edit the component to print your answers, then Run. Remember: groups (parentheses) are invisible and [brackets] are dynamic.
codeLab.expectedOutput: Your predicted URL for each file path.
hints: A folder name is a path segment unless it's wrapped in parentheses (a route group).
[brackets] mark a dynamic segment that captures a value from the URL.

keyTakeaways: A folder adds a route segment, and a `page.
A dynamic folder such as `[slug]` matches different values in one part of a route.
A route group can organize related files without adding the group name to the public URL.
